item.title: The Ultimate Guide to Making 2027 Your Best Year Yet
item.dc:creator: Margaret Cole
item.description: The nine steps you need to start your 2027 off right.
item.content:encoded:
If you’re like me, when December rolls around each year, you insist that the next year is finally going to be your year. You make Pinterest boards and set a few ambitious goals, but then somehow you look back 6 months later and realize that none of it actually stuck.

Yearning to finally break the cycle? In this article you’ll find everything you need to actually make 2027 your best year yet. By the end, you’ll have your goals, themes for the year, a clear vision, and action steps to carry it all out. This guidebook is exhaustive, so take as little or as much as you need. And if you need a practical example of each of these steps as you’re reading, take a look at Step 8 for my personal 2027 plan.

Step 1: Look back before you leap forward

A successful plan starts by acknowledging where you are now. 2026 surely had its ups and its downs. You may have built habits that make you feel amazing and then others that you know deep down you could do without. So, before you decide what your vision for 2027 is, you must reflect on your current state.

Spend a few minutes and reflect on any of the questions below that you feel drawn to:

  • What was my proudest accomplishment this year?
  • What was the best decision I made this year?
  • Which moments brought me the most joy?
  • What new skill, habit, or mindset did I build that I want to keep?
  • What is one habit I want to stop doing?
  • What was the biggest obstacle I faced, and how did I navigate it?
  • What mistake or setback taught me the most valuable lesson?
  • Where did I spend too much time, energy, or money without getting much in return?
  • What is one thing I was afraid to do at the start of the year that feels easy now?
  • What project or task gave me the greatest sense of purpose?
  • When did I feel most burnt out, and what triggered it?
  • Did my daily actions align with my long-term goals?

Want more questions to choose from? Pick a Card has 24 more, free on the site.

With that, you should now be adequately equipped to look onward towards 2027.

Step 2: Choose your themes and your word

Rather than immediately setting 20+ ambitious goals for 2027, we’re going to start the process by choosing a few focus areas to improve this next year. Here are six areas to choose from:

  • Health: how you move, eat, sleep, and feel in your body
  • Career: your work, your growth, and where you want to go next
  • Money: what you earn, save, and spend
  • Relationships: friends, family, and your romantic relationships
  • Learning: new skills, books, classes, and anything you’re curious about
  • Fun: hobbies, travel, and anything that is purely for joy

Now I want you to look back at your answers from Step 1. Which areas kept coming up, whether as something that drained you or something that lit you up? Those are your clues. Choose the three that feel most important to you right now. For example, if burnout was your biggest obstacle this year, health might be one. If you’re ready for a promotion or a pivot, career might be another. And if you realized you’ve barely had any fun, fun might make the list.

One thing to keep in mind. You might want to focus on improving in each of the categories I outlined above, and that is great, but in order to make sustainable and noteworthy progress, I want you to really hone in on just a few categories for now. Being selective here will allow you to really focus your energy and allow you to actually remember your categories months from now. If you can’t say your themes out loud without checking your notes, there are too many.

Have your themes? Now it’s time to choose your word.

Your word is the one-word version of your year. It isn’t a goal, so you can’t fail it. Think of it as a filter you can hold your decisions up to: does this fit my word? Some popular ones are rest, courage, consistency, ease, bold, and enough. The best words are short, feel a little exciting, and sound like something you’d actually say to yourself on a hard day.

If you’re feeling stuck, try asking yourself:

  • What do I want more of next year?
  • What do I want less of?
  • How do I want to feel on an ordinary Tuesday?
  • What would the version of me at the end of 2027 thank me for?

Still can’t land on one? Use VIRI’s 2027 word generator below. Pick a few answers, hit generate, and keep going until one feels right.

The word generator is interactive, so it lives on the website. Find your 2027 word on vitalityritual.org.

By the end of this step, you should have a few themes and one word. Write them somewhere you’ll see them every day, because we’ll use them in every step that follows.

Step 3: Goal setting that survives a bad week

Most goals don’t fail because you stop caring. They fail because of a bad week. You get sick, work gets chaotic, or you travel, and suddenly you’re behind on a goal that only works if everything goes right. So you decide you’ve failed and quit altogether. This step is about setting goals for your worst week, not your best one.

What we’re going to do next is write out 1-2 goals for each of your themes. Here’s what makes a goal that lasts:

  • Make it specific. “Get healthier” can’t be checked off. “Strength train three times a week” can.
  • Focus on what you do, not what happens. You can’t fully control whether you get the promotion, but you can control whether you ask for a stretch project every quarter. Aim for the part that’s in your hands.
  • Give it a bad-week version. Write your normal version and the smallest version that still counts. Normal: three workouts a week. Bad week: one ten-minute walk. The goal is to never drop to zero.
  • Internally, add one sentence on why. Why does this matter to you? On day 90, when the excitement has worn off, this is what you’ll remember.

Here’s what that might look like:

  • Health: Strength train three times a week. Bad week: one ten-minute walk.
  • Career: Spend one hour a week on something that builds my skills. Bad week: ten minutes.
  • Fun: Plan one thing a week just for me. Bad week: put on a favorite movie.

Once you have your goals, test each one. Could you still do the bad-week version on your worst day? If not, make it smaller. And when you do miss a day, don’t spiral. Just don’t miss twice. One missed day is a blip. Two is the start of a new habit.

By the end of this step, you should have multiple specific goals, each with a normal version, a bad-week version, and a reason why. Keep them right next to your themes and your word.

Step 4: Build your 2027 vision board

As a girl with a million Pinterest boards for every mood, every season, and every dream, this might be my favorite part. A few years ago, I made a physical vision board where I cut out dozens of photos and quotes and strategically placed them onto a poster board. I hung up my board on the wall in front of my bed so that every morning when I woke up, it was the first thing I saw.

Having a visual reminder of your goals is one of the greatest ways you can honor them. A vision board you’re proud of though takes time. Start the process today but feel free to come back to it later.

Create a Pinterest board called “2027.” Next, spend some time going through Pinterest and adding every photo that resonates with how you envision your 2027. Think through what your perfect day would look like and find pins associated with every aspect of it. Remember your themes. Find cute photos of your 2027 word. Do you want your 2027 to be associated with a certain color? Find quotes that inspire you. Add it all to the board. By the end, you should have a solid 50-100 pins saved.

Now comes the crafty portion. Start by getting yourself a poster board, any size works. I’m planning on making mine either 16x20” or 22x28.” Next, go through your Pinterest board and save every photo that you think you’d want on your vision board to a Google or Word doc. When you save the photos, make them different sizes depending on how much emphasis you want them to have on your board. It’s no fun if all your photos are the same size. You should have a solid 5-6 pages worth of photos by the end of this step. Print out your doc and cut out each of your pictures.

It’s now time to assemble your board. Put all your photos onto your poster board and play around with where each one goes. Try swapping in other photos depending on sizing until you have a mock-up that you absolutely love. The final step is to glue or tape everything to your board.

You should now have a beautifully assembled vision board. Hang it up on your wall, put it on your desk. The important part is that your board is in a spot that you’ll see every day.

Step 5: Habits and systems

Your goals tell you where you’re going. Your habits are how you actually get there. Here’s the part nobody tells you: motivation makes a terrible plan. It shows up in January, disappears by March, and definitely can’t be counted on during a random Wednesday. What you can count on is a system that works even when you don’t feel like it.

A system is just a small, repeatable setup that makes your goals the default instead of a decision. Here’s how to build one:

Attach it to something you already do. This is called habit stacking. Instead of “I’ll read more,” try “After I get into bed, I’ll read ten pages.” Or “After I pour my morning coffee, I’ll write down my top three goals for the day.” Your existing routines become the reminder, so you never have to remember.

Make the first step ridiculously easy. Lay out your workout clothes the night before. Put your book on your pillow. Charge your phone across the room. Every bit of friction you remove is one less thing you have to talk yourself into.

Start small. Remember the bad-week versions from Step 3? That’s where you begin. A tiny habit you do every day beats a big one you do twice. Once it feels automatic, you can always do more.

Track it somewhere you’ll see it. A habit tracker, a calendar you X off each day, or a note on your phone all work. Seeing a streak builds momentum, and seeing a gap is your cue to get back on before it turns into two missed days.

Add a weekly reset. Pick one 15-minute slot each week (Sunday evening works well) to look at your themes, your word, and the week ahead. What’s coming up that might make your goals harder? What’s the smallest version you’ll commit to if it gets busy? Then once a month, ask what’s working, what isn’t, and adjust. A plan that never changes eventually gets abandoned.

One last thing: resist the urge to start everything on January 1st. Pick one or two habits to begin with and add the next one once the first feels automatic. We’ll map that out in the next step.

By the end of this step, you should have a trigger and a tracker for each of your goals, plus a weekly reset on your calendar.

Step 6: Your 2027 calendar

A plan that only lives in your head is just a wish. This step is about getting your year onto an actual calendar, so you can stop reacting to 2027 and start planning for it. Open your calendar, whether that’s Google Calendar or a paper planner, and work through these in order:

Block out what’s already happening. Birthdays, weddings, trips, work deadlines, races, and the months you already know will be chaotic. Seeing your whole year in one place shows you when you’ll have room for something new and when you won’t. If you know October is going to be slammed, don’t plan to start something big in October.

Give each quarter one milestone per theme. Look at your goals from Step 3 and ask yourself what progress would look like by the end of March, June, September, and December. Keep it small. For example, Health: three workouts a week for a full month. Career: finish the first project that builds my skills. Fun: book one trip or event for later in the year. A quarter is long enough to see real change and short enough that you won’t forget about it.

Stagger your start dates. Here’s where we map out the “don’t start everything on January 1st” rule from Step 5. Choose one or two habits to begin in January, then put the next start dates on your calendar for February, March, and so on. Each new habit begins once the last one feels automatic.

Schedule your check-ins. Add your weekly reset from Step 5 as a recurring event. Then add a monthly check-in and a quarterly review at the end of each quarter, where you look at your milestones, see what worked, and adjust. Changing the plan isn’t failing. It’s the whole point.

Plan your rest. Block off a few days, or even a full week, for downtime before the year fills up. If you wait until you need a break, you’ll feel guilty taking it. Think back to when you felt most burnt out in Step 1, and plan a break before that time of year comes around again.

By the end of this step, you should have your year mapped out: key dates, a milestone for each theme every quarter, staggered start dates for your habits, and your check-ins on the calendar.

Step 7: The “not doing” list

Every planning guide tells you what to add. Almost none tell you what to take away. But you’ll have the same 24 hours in 2027 that you had in 2026, so if you’re adding goals and habits, something has to make room for them. That’s what this list is for.

A “not doing” list is a short list of things you’re deliberately choosing to stop, so your plan actually fits into your real life. Here’s how to make yours:

Start with Step 1. Look back at your answers to “What is one habit I want to stop doing?” and “Where did I spend too much time, energy, or money without getting much in return?” Then think about when you felt burnt out. Those answers are the first things on your list.

Keep it short. Aim for three to five items. A list of fifteen is just another to-do list that makes you feel guilty.

Make each one specific. “Stop wasting time” can’t be checked. “No phone in bed” can. A few others: no saying yes to plans I don’t actually want to go to, no buying things just because they’re on sale, no checking my work email after 7 PM.

Give each one a replacement. If you remove a habit without replacing it, it leaves a gap, and the old habit will happily fill it back in. If you’re giving up your phone in bed, decide what you’ll do instead. Remember “After I get into bed, I’ll read ten pages” from Step 5? That’s your replacement.

Hold new commitments up to your word. When you’re invited to something or tempted to take on a new project, ask the question from Step 2: does this fit my word? Does it support one of my themes? If not, it’s a no, or at least a “not right now.” Saying no isn’t selfish. It’s how you protect the things you actually said matter.

Add it to the spot where you keep your themes, your word, and your goals.

By the end of this step, you should have three to five things you’re letting go of in 2027, each with a replacement, and a simple filter for saying no to everything else.

Step 8: My 2027, as an example

A guidebook isn’t much help without a real example, right? So let’s go through all 7 steps together.

Step 1: Look back

There was a lot from 2026 that I can look back on proudly. I graduated from college, started my first full-time job, moved into my own apartment in my dream city, was financially independent, ran a marathon, signed up for another, deepened my relationship, got a cat, traveled…a lot, started VIRI, read for fun, and am almost done applying for grad school. What a year!

But there is still absolutely room for improvement. I wasn’t as financially responsible as I would have hoped, my routine ebbed and flowed, I frequently forgot to prioritize friends and family, and my nutrition was often a second thought.

Step 2: Themes and 2027 word

Based on where I am at now and where I hope to be by the end of 2027, my themes are going to be: health, money, and learning.

Health: 2027 is going to be a huge year physically for me. I have highly ambitious marathon goals. And as you may have read in one of my previous articles, marathon training really does influence your entire lifestyle, and so there is a lot in the health category that needs my dedication and attention in 2027.

Money: it’s time to finally prioritize saving. No more impulse buying. No more living above my means. If I want to accomplish my long-term goals, financial stability must be a priority.

Learning: I’m currently in the process of applying to grad school. If I get accepted and decide to go, this will change a lot of my day-to-day life. And outside of grad school, reading has become highly important, but something I have not spent enough time on.

And that leads me to my 2027 word: INVEST.

Step 3: Goal setting

  • Health: By prioritizing consistency and perseverance in my training, I will run a 3:20 marathon in April.
  • Health: I will drink 64oz of water per day and eat vegetables with at least one meal per day.
  • Money: I will invest at least $10,000 into my brokerage account in 2027.
  • Money: I will wait at least one week before making purchases of over $50.
  • Learning: I will read at least one book per month.
  • Learning: I will complete my Wharton certificate and either enroll in grad school or find an alternative.

Step 4: Vision board

Stay tuned for the finished product, but here are the pins currently on my 2027 vision board.

Step 5: Habits and systems

Here are a few of the habits that I am setting for myself in order to accomplish my goals and stick to my 2027 themes.

I will read, even just 5 pages, before I go to bed each night.

I will get out the door within 45 minutes of waking up each morning, even if I don’t complete my full planned workout. It’s better to run any distance than to not have run at all.

I will create a physical log-book for my marathon training. Being able to record my progress in a physical book will keep me motivated, show me how far I’ve gone, and make me more likely to run on the days I don’t want to.

I will create a physical log of my savings progress. A budget tracker, a log of how much money I put aside each month. Right now I’m not tracking this in any metric, which creates a lack of accountability. I will spend 10 minutes each week filling out my financial log.

I will plan my meals around vegetables rather than the main course. When I go to the grocery store, I will pick up my vegetables first.

These are just a few of the systems and habits I would like to implement in the new year, as they relate to my goals and themes. I am sure they will change, but simply starting is the first step.

Step 6: Your 2027 calendar

I’m keeping my real calendar to myself, so here’s a mock January built from everything above: marathon training four days a week with long runs on Saturdays, strength training on Mondays, my budget check and meal prep on Sundays, and reading before bed every night.

Step 7: “Not doing”

And finally, we have the “not doing” list. In 2026, while I ultimately accomplished many of my goals, travel and chaotic weeks threw a wrench in many of my plans. And so, in 2027, I am NOT allowing abnormal weeks to dictate my routines. Instead, by keeping a calendar and always planning for the future, I will account for when weeks are crazy and readjust my goals accordingly. I will continue to make progress rather than giving up my routines altogether.

In 2027, I am also NOT making heat-of-the-moment purchases. When I want to buy something, I will sit and think it over for a period of time before making the decision.

Want to fill out your own? Here’s a blank one-page version of this whole plan to print: your word, your themes, your goals, and your first habit. Download the one-page plan.

Step 9: Start this week

You now have a plan, but a plan only works once you act on it. Don’t wait for January 1st. The best time to start is while the idea still feels exciting, so here are four small things to do in the next seven days.

Put your themes and your word where you’ll see them every day. Write them on a sticky note for your mirror, your desk, or the lock screen of your phone. Mine says INVEST, and I’ll be looking at it every morning.

Pick your first habit and attach it to a trigger. Just one. Use the “After I…, I will…” format from Step 5, and start it this week instead of waiting for a perfect Monday.

Put your weekly reset on your calendar. Make it a recurring event, so you never have to remember to schedule it. Fifteen minutes, same time every week.

Start building your 2027 vision board. Even five pins is enough. You can keep adding to it all year.

That’s it. You’re not trying to build a perfect year. You’re building one with a foundation of consistency and progress. If the plan stops fitting, change it. That’s what your weekly resets and quarterly reviews are for.

I’d love to know your word for 2027. Tell me in the comments, or send it to me on Instagram.

Here’s to your best year yet.
